accuracy.evidence: Slip, misconception and misread are distinguished as in error-analysis practice: a slip is a careless error on known material, a misconception is a held wrong idea (0.25 > 0.5, heavy things always sink). The hypercorrection claim matches Butterfield and Metcalfe (2001): high-confidence errors are corrected more often after feedback. Hattie ranks feedback among the strongest influences; the EEF metacognition guidance covers plan, monitor and evaluate.

misconceptions.evidence: Tackles the common slips: treating every error as carelessness so misconceptions never get fixed, rubbing out work before looking, redoing everything rather than the repeating error, reading a mistake as proof of being stupid. The adult notes call out the parent slip of giving the answer straight away. Mastery item m8 checks that a misconception needs relearning, not just a slower check.

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab mixes tapping the faulty line inside three worked answers (carry, a misread '5 more than', a spelling rule), a three-way kind sort, a marked test whose tally bars build up as each wrong answer is opened, an order-the-moves board and a thoughts sort with a hypercorrection prediction. No other flagship lab does line-by-line error finding or cause tallies.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step practises a real error-analysis move: spot the wrong line, name the cause, count which cause repeats and choose what to practise, order spot / find why / fix / try a new one, then pick helpful thoughts. Feedback explains why each choice is right or wrong, e.g. 'They know the fact. Rushing caused it, so it is a slip.'

predictions.evidence: Learners predict whether to rub out or look first before step 0, choose between practising everything or the repeating mistake before tallying Ava's test, and predict whether a sure-and-wrong answer is remembered better or worse before the hypercorrection reveal. Each prediction is checked by what the lab then shows.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The Challenge gives five fresh scenarios (rushed 8 x 5, misread question, wrong idea, hiding work, skipping the why) with instant reasons per answer and an end summary of the four moves. Wrong choices name the kind of mistake and the matching fix rather than just saying 'try again'.

readability.evidence: Kid text is FK grade 1.0 with short sentences and words like 'rushed', 'wrong idea', 'missed what the question asked'. Adult notes are FK 9.6 and define each term (error analysis, slip, misconception, misread, hypercorrection, metacognition) in plain words. Lab buttons use two-word labels.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph does a job: why to look before rubbing out, how to find the line, the three kinds with their fixes, and the repeat-first rule. The adult notes give research, terms, common mistakes and a lab summary. No stock openers or vague praise; examples are concrete sums and sentences.

mobile.evidence: Checked at 360x640 light and iPhone 13 dark. Test rows span the full width so no text spills, tally bars sit under the list, sort bins fit three across with short sub-labels, and every step has big tap buttons as well as drag. A real touch drag dropped cards into bins and order slots.

accessibility.evidence: Canvas has a live aria-label that reads the feedback (e.g. 'Yes, Helps me learn. Next: ...'); every drag has a button alternative; colours come from the theme palette and the axe check passes in light and dark. Bins pair colour with text labels so meaning never relies on colour alone.

Metcalfe, J. (2017) Learning from errors, Annual Review of Psychology 68
